sections.h2: Where is the Hardin County Recorder in Kenton?
sections.html:
The Hardin County Recorder is at One Courthouse Square, Suite 220, Kenton, Ohio 43326. Dial 419-674-2252 or 419-674-2250, or fax 419-675-2802. The counter opens at half past eight and closes at four on weekdays.

The Auditor is in the same courthouse, Suite 250, at 419-674-2239, and keeps hours of 8:00 to 4:00 on weekdays. Since a conveyance has to touch both offices, a short walk down the hall is often how a deed gets done.

The Recorder's page links to an online search run through Kofile, and it points visitors to the Ohio Recorders' Association site for more fee information. The office also says plainly that it keeps the vital records of land ownership and of every lien against it, which is why a clean recorded deed matters to the next buyer.

sections.h2: What is Hardin County, Ohio, made of?
sections.html:
Hardin County lies in west central Ohio and Kenton is both seat and biggest city. The legislature created it in 1820, it was organized in 1833, and its name honors John Hardin, a Revolutionary War officer. Land area comes to 470 square miles and borders Hancock, Wyandot, Marion, Union, Logan, Auglaize and Allen counties.

It is a small, mostly rural county. The 2020 census put 56.4% of residents in rural areas, and the population has slipped from 32,058 in 2010 to 30,696 at the 2020 count and about 30,072 by July 2025.

  • Owner-occupied housing rate: 74.7% (2020 to 2024).
  • Typical owner-reported home value: $151,200.
  • Median gross rent: $793, and 12,944 housing units.
  • Median household income: $62,484, and mean commute of 23.6 minutes.
  • Building permits in 2025: 24.

Numbers come from QuickFacts for Hardin County, and Wikipedia supplies geography and founding.

sections.h2: What do Hardin County's housing numbers mean for a seller?
sections.html:
The 2020 census counted 12,883 housing units in the county, with 9.7% of them vacant. Of the occupied homes, 71.3% were owner-occupied and 28.7% rented, with 10.0% of rentals sitting empty. There were 11,638 households, and about 28.3% of them were people living alone.

In a county with this many single-person households and a falling population, a house that sits listed for a while is not unusual. A sale to someone paying cash and closing at a local title office still ends with the same Auditor stamp and the same Recorder filing, so the deed steps in this guide apply to either route.

sections.h2: Why must a Hardin County deed carry the Auditor's stamp?
sections.html:
A mailed conveyance is taken only when the Auditor's stamp is already on it. The office says it will not walk a conveyance through the map department and the Auditor's office for you.

That sets the order: map department and Auditor first, Recorder last. A seller who mails a deed straight to the Recorder should expect it to come back unrecorded. A seller who lives far away can hand that errand to the attorney or title agent running the closing.

On the Auditor's forms page you will find the DTE 100 value statement, the DTE 100EX exemption statement and the DTE 101 homestead conveyance statement, with a reminder to confirm the newest version with the Ohio Department of Taxation.

sections.h2: What does a Hardin County recording run?
sections.html:
The recording fee comes from state statute, and the Recorder's page refers readers to the state recorders' association for rates. ORC 317.32 builds the opening pair of pages from a $17 base fee and a $17 housing trust fund fee, with $4 and $4 for each page that follows.

The statute also lets a county charge a document preservation surcharge of up to $5. The Recorders' Association table, revised October 24, 2024, lists $34.00 up front for two pages and $8.00 for each extra page, and notes a surcharge not exceeding $5.00 per document may be added. Call the Hardin County Recorder at either of its two numbers to learn exactly what the county adds per document, and keep the receipt with your closing papers.

sections.h2: What must happen to a deed before Kenton will record it?
sections.html:
The seller signs and then acknowledges the deed in front of an authorized official. Under ORC 5301.01 that can be a judge or clerk of a court of record, a county auditor, a county engineer, a notary public or a mayor, who certifies the acknowledgment.

Many sellers visit a notary at a title company or bank. The deed then goes to the Auditor with a completed DTE 100, or a DTE 100EX for an exempt transfer. Ask the Hardin County Auditor for the conveyance rate and per-parcel transfer fee, since counties differ.

ORC 317.114 sets the page format here as in every Ohio county: legible print, black or blue ink, no highlighting, and empty space at the head of the page for county stamps.

sections.h2: What does the Hardin County Auditor handle for a manufactured home sale?
sections.html:
Homes of the manufactured or mobile kind that are taxed like real property use their own set of forms. The Auditor posts a registration certificate (DTE 41), a conveyance fee statement of value and receipt (DTE 100M), and an exemption statement (DTE 100MEX) for that category.

A refund or waiver application for destroyed or damaged manufactured homes (DTE 49) is posted too. When the home sits on land you own, ask the Auditor whether your sale takes the real property forms, the manufactured home forms, or both.

The Real Estate section adds the 2 1/2% reduction application (DTE 105C), the valuation complaint (DTE 1) and a deduction application for damaged or destroyed property (DTE 26). Ask about the 2 1/2% reduction at closing if the buyer will make the house a primary home.

sections.h2: How do Hardin County tax dates affect a sale?
sections.html:
The Auditor acts as the county's chief assessor, and its page describes a full reappraisal of real property every six years with an update every three. Find out where your parcel sits in that cycle, because a new value can change the tax bills a buyer inherits.

On the Auditor's calendar, February 11 is the last day to pay the first half of the real estate bill without penalty and July 8 is the last day for the second half. The same calendar opens the Board of Revision complaint period on January 3 and closes it March 31. Homestead and 2 1/2% rollback applications are listed as due in early June. Check your current tax bill for exact dates, since weekends and holidays can move them.

  • Learn from the closing agent how taxes will be prorated.
  • Ask whether the parcel has a homestead reduction, because DTE 101 then travels with the deed.
  • Photograph the stamped deed before it goes to the Recorder.

faqs.q: Can a deed go by mail to the Hardin County Recorder?
faqs.a: Only if the Auditor's stamp is already on it. Without that stamp the Recorder's Office will not take the conveyance, and it does not walk deeds through the map department or Auditor.

faqs.q: When is the Hardin County Recorder open?
faqs.a: It opens at half past eight each weekday morning and closes at 4:00 p.m., at One Courthouse Square, Suite 220 in Kenton.

faqs.q: Who can notarize a deed in Ohio?
faqs.a: Under ORC 5301.01 a notary public, a county auditor, a county engineer, a mayor, or a judge or clerk of a court of record can take the acknowledgment. Most sellers use a notary.

faqs.q: Is there a Hardin County online records search?
faqs.a: Yes. The Recorder's page links to an online service and search provided through Kofile.

faqs.q: Who tells me the Hardin County conveyance fee?
faqs.a: The Auditor, at 419-674-2239. That office collects the conveyance and transfer fees before the deed moves on to the Recorder.
